commands.short: Open the tkt agent, a chat that drives your tickets
commands.long:
tkt agent opens a chat in this pane about the repository's tickets. It runs
pi, a coding agent that release builds of tkt carry inside them (MIT licensed,
https://github.com/earendil-works/pi), with only tkt's own extension. Running
tkt with no arguments opens it too, when you type it at a terminal in a herdr
pane inside a repository with the lifecycle configuration.

Say what you want in plain words: "start ACM-12", "run ACM-13 to ACM-15 in
auto with sol", "I approved the plan for ACM-12, continue", "ACM-12 is merged,
remove it". Starting tickets and stages runs in the background and the prompt
comes back at once, so you can start the next ticket while the first one
plans. A board pinned to the top of the chat shows every ticket, and on top
what needs you: a plan to approve, a question from its agent, a pull request
ready for human verification, or a tkt auto loop that paused for you. The chat
scrolls below the board, so it covers nothing. An item leaves the board as
soon as its ticket moves on, and the chat stays free of them. Each new one
also shows a herdr notification. Each row shows what the branch changes,
such as +293 -8, and the pull request's title, and marks a chore's run. When
a status page reports an incident, the board says so at its top. /board hide
and /board show put the board away and back.

Ask how a ticket went, merged ones too: "how did ACM-12 go?", "what failed
in ACM-12 and ACM-13?". The chat reads tkt history: each step with its time,
and the pull request's commits and reviews with the review bot's findings.

The same actions work without the model as slash commands: /suggest (a
suggest tab where suggest-tickets picks tickets to start next; add what you
want, such as /suggest five tickets tagged feedback, or type it when /suggest
alone asks), /start (add "as
PRESET" for a preset), /approve, /next, /auto, /hold, /sync, /send, /show,
/peek (the agent's live screen), /run (a stage in a fresh session),
/relaunch (tkt resume), /check (the human verification checklist, which
offers to sync a ticket that is behind first), /done, /inbox (what needs
you, with fixed answers), /dismiss (set aside what a ticket needs from you),
/board (every ticket in columns), /chores (the
repository's chores; /chores run NAME starts a run now), /history, /stats,
/version, /update and /web (the same chat in your browser, mirrored both
ways; tkt help web). A tool that changes a ticket your message did
not name asks first, and removing a ticket always asks. Text for a working
agent goes in at once, and the agent reads it at its next step; text for an
agent that asks a question waits until you answer it in its tab.

The chat checks for a newer tkt release when it opens and every six hours,
and names it under the board. /update installs it with tkt update, then offers
to quit: the chat runs the old tkt until you reopen it with the command it
prints. A development build gets no notice, and /update does not replace it.
/version says which tkt and pi the chat runs, and whether the tkt on disk is
another one now, as after tkt update or a new build.

Tickets in auto run in tkt auto loops that outlive the chat, so they keep
moving, and notify you, after you close it. A loop that pauses for you goes on
by itself once you act, such as answering the agent in its tab. tkt agent also
starts tkt watch for the repository when none runs, which takes the upkeep
steps for every ticket: it syncs a moved base, fixes failing checks once per
head, and removes a ticket once finish-ticket merged it. The board's heading
says watch on or watch off.

The chat is apart from any pi you run yourself. It reads none of ~/.pi/agent:
not your extensions, skills, prompt templates or themes, and not the project's
AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md. It keeps its own settings, logins and sessions in
${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-~/.config}/tkt/pi. Log in to a model provider once with
/login inside the chat.

The chat brings two themes of its own, tkt-dark and tkt-light, and picks the
one that suits the terminal's background. Overlays such as /board and /peek
draw on a panel of their own, so they read well on a transparent terminal. A
theme you pick in /settings wins from then on.

pi runs in the repository's root, where it keeps the sessions, so --continue
picks up the last chat about this repository from any of its worktrees. When
you quit, the chat prints the command that resumes it: tkt agent --session
ID. Flags after -- go to pi as they are, such as tkt agent -- --thinking high;
pi --help lists them.

In config.toml, an [agent] table picks the model and loads more pi extensions,
such as one that adds a model provider (tkt help config). --model overrides the
model for one run. Without [agent] model, pi starts on its own default: in
/model, press Ctrl+S on a model to make it the default for new chats.

tkt unpacks the bundled pi the first time, under
${XDG_DATA_HOME:-~/.local/share}/tkt/pi. Set TKT_PI to run another pi binary
instead; tkt doctor shows which pi tkt agent runs.

tkt agent replaces itself with pi, so it needs a terminal and prints no result.
--dry-run prints how it would start pi, and with --json the exact command line
and environment.
commands.example:
tkt agent
  tkt agent --continue
  tkt agent --session 01a15a4d
  tkt agent --model acme/large
  tkt agent -- --thinking high
  tkt agent --dry-run --json

commands.short: Open the tkt agent's web page, a browser view of the chat
commands.long:
tkt web opens the tkt agent's web page in your browser: the same chat as tkt
agent, mirrored both ways. A message you send in either place shows in both,
with the model's answer as it streams in, its tool calls, and the times. A
question the chat asks, such as "Remove ACM-12?", shows in both, and the first
answer wins. Slash commands work in the page as in the terminal.

The page lives inside a running chat, which serves it on 127.0.0.1 only. The
first chat in a repository serves it; a second one says it serves none. When
no chat serves the page, tkt web opens tkt agent in a new tab of this herdr
workspace, waits for its page, and opens that. Outside herdr it refuses: run
tkt agent in a herdr pane, then /web in the chat. When you quit the chat, the
page says so and comes back by itself once a chat serves it again.

The address carries a token, which the page keeps in a cookie, so another web
page in your browser cannot drive the chat. tkt web prints the address, so
--no-open gives it to you without a browser.

The page follows your system's light or dark setting until you pick one with
its sun and moon button. It keeps that choice in
${XDG_STATE_HOME:-~/.local/state}/tkt/web.json for every repository.

pi's own screens, such as /model, /login, /settings, /resume and /tree, open
in the terminal only. Text you have typed but not sent stays where you typed
it.
commands.example:
tkt web
  tkt web --no-open --json
  tkt web --dry-run

flags.name: dry-run
flags.usage: print what tkt web would run instead of running it

flags.name: no-open
flags.usage: print the page's address without opening a browser

commands.short: Ask a fresh agent in the suggest tab which tickets to start next
commands.long:
tkt suggest has the suggest-tickets skill pick the next tickets to start.
It opens a suggest tab at the repository's root, or reuses it, starts a
fresh session there, and sends it what you ask, after the skill's name:

  tkt suggest five tickets tagged feedback
  -> Use the suggest-tickets skill for this request: five tickets tagged
     feedback

suggest-tickets takes the number your request names, and narrows the
candidates by what else it says, such as a label, an area or a model. With
no words, or only a count, tkt sends the suggest line for that many tickets,
3 by default:

  Use the suggest-tickets skill to suggest the next 3 tickets to start, ones
  that can run side by side.

suggest-tickets only reads. It lists the ready tickets, keeps the ones
whose blockers are all done, and ranks them by how many tickets wait on
each, then by priority. It drops one that would collide with work in
flight, judged from the files each in-flight branch changes, or with
another pick, and with model routing on it takes at most one heavy ticket.
It reports what waits on you first, then the picks and what it left out,
and ends with a line such as

  Suggested: ACM-14 (frontier), ACM-21 (acme-small-2)

The session runs on the [suggest] preset (tkt help config), or the default
preset; --as picks another, such as a cheap one.

tkt suggest returns once the agent has the prompt, and reads nothing it
says. The answer stays in the tab: read it there, ask the agent about it,
and start the tickets you want with tkt start, adding --as PRESET for a
ticket whose model another preset serves. The tkt agent's /suggest opens
the same tab.
commands.example:
tkt suggest
  tkt suggest 5
  tkt suggest five tickets tagged feedback that can run side by side
  tkt suggest 'tickets for the fast preset' --as fast --json

flags.usage: run the agent on PRESET instead of the [suggest] one

commands.short: Create the worktree and tab, start an agent and send it the prompt
commands.long:
tkt start creates or reuses the ticket's worktree through worktrunk, opens a
herdr tab named after the ticket, starts an agent in build mode (Claude Code
with --dangerously-skip-permissions, OpenCode on its Build agent) and sends it
the prompt, typically the dispatcher's start-ticket block.

A new branch starts from the base on the remote, such as origin/main: tkt
fetches it first, so the plan starts from the code the base holds now. When
the fetch fails, the branch starts from the local base.

The ticket's tab gets TMPDIR set to a private directory, such as
/tmp/tkt-acme-app-ACM-12-123456, so agents of two tickets never write the
same temporary file. Every tab tkt opens for the ticket gets the same one,
and tkt done removes it. OpenCode runs its tools in its own service, outside
the tab, so its agents get the directory through tkt's plugin (tkt help
hook).

Without an ID, tkt start takes the first ticket id in the prompt; with both,
they must match. Without a prompt, it sends the start stage line. --prompt -
reads the prompt from stdin, which keeps a long prompt out of your shell
history; --prompt-file reads it from a file.

The prompt's Model: line, when it has one, picks the preset (tkt help config);
--as picks one yourself.

tkt start refuses when an agent already runs in the worktree: use tkt run for
a fresh session, or tkt resume to bring back the last one. When the agent stops
at a startup dialog, answer it in the tab and rerun the same tkt start: it
continues where it stopped.

--scratch NAME starts work that has no ticket. tkt start makes the worktree
and branch NAME and a tab named NAME, starts the agent and sends it nothing.
NAME takes letters, digits, '-' and '_', and must not be a ticket id. Other
tkt commands work on tickets only, so they do not see this worktree; remove
it with wt remove NAME.
commands.example:
xclip -selection clipboard -o | tkt start --prompt -
  tkt start ACM-12
  tkt start ACM-12 --prompt-file plan-request.md --as fast
  tkt start ACM-12 --dry-run
  tkt start --scratch spike-login --as fast

commands.short: Approve the plan in the ticket's own session, so work-ticket begins
commands.long:
tkt approve tells the ticket's planning session that you approve its plan. The
same session then goes on with work-ticket, so the plan it wrote stays in its
context. tkt run would start a fresh session and lose it.

Read the plan first with tkt show ID. tkt approve refuses unless the agent is
idle and its last status line since your last message is
Status: AWAITING_APPROVAL; --force sends the approval anyway. To ask for
changes instead, use tkt send ID "what to change".

tkt approve resets the round count that tkt auto caps.
commands.example:
tkt show ACM-12
  tkt approve ACM-12
  tkt approve ACM-12 --dry-run

commands.short: Type text into the ticket's running session, which keeps its conversation
commands.long:
tkt send types text into the ticket's running session and waits until the
agent takes it. The session keeps its whole conversation, so use it to ask for
changes to a plan, or to answer a question the agent asked in its last
message.

It refuses while the agent works (tkt wait blocks until it is done) and while
it waits in its own dialog, such as a question with options: typed text does
not reach that dialog, so answer it in the ticket's tab. tkt show ID --screen
prints what the dialog asks.

--steer types the text in while the agent works, to steer it mid-task.
Claude Code and OpenCode hold the text and read it at their next step; the
result says steered. A question in the agent's dialog still refuses it.

--wait queues the text instead: tkt send waits until the agent stops working,
stops waiting on its own background task, and has no question open, then
types the text in. With --steer, it waits only for the question to close. It
holds no lock while it waits, so tkt auto and the other commands go on.

To start a stage in a fresh session instead, use tkt run. To approve a plan,
use tkt approve.
commands.example:
tkt send ACM-12 "Keep the old endpoint and drop step 4 of the plan."
  tkt send ACM-12 --steer "Stop: the endpoint stays. Drop step 4."
  tkt send ACM-12 --prompt-file answer.md

commands.short: Drive the ticket until it needs you: approve, review, fix, until READY_FOR_HUMAN
commands.long:
tkt auto drives one ticket through the lifecycle and pauses where a person
decides. It reads the same facts as tkt ls, then:

  - starts the ticket when it has no worktree yet, on --as PRESET when given;
    with --approve-plan its start line says the run is unattended, so
    start-ticket skips the browser plan presentation and asks every open
    question with the harness's question tool;
  - waits while the agent works, or waits on its own background task such
    as a CI watcher;
  - approves the plan when start-ticket ends with AWAITING_APPROVAL, but only
    with --approve-plan; without it the loop pauses there for you;
  - waits for CI, then for the review bot in CI to review the new head;
  - merges a moved base itself when the merge is clean, as tkt sync does,
    with no agent and no fix round; on a conflict it runs resolve, which only
    merges and resolves (it runs git merge-tree on each look to tell the
    two apart);
  - runs address on findings, and ci when checks fail, each in a fresh
    session;
  - once the head is reviewed clean (the bot's CLEAR, or review-pr's
    READY_FOR_HUMAN; review-pr runs only in a repository with no review bot,
    [review] bot_wait = "0s"), runs verify where workflow.md turns agent
    verification on: verify-pr runs the human verification steps and posts
    what it saw. A step it reports failed gets an address run, which counts
    as a fix round, then a new review and a new verify;
  - ends with success when the head is reviewed clean and, with agent
    verification on, verify-pr passed every step or could not run some.

Without --yolo it never merges and never removes a worktree.

--yolo carries the ticket to the merge with nobody watching. It runs only
where workflow.md turns on autonomous runs, agent verification and plan
review, and refuses with autonomous_off naming the rows that are off. A
yolo run starts with the ticket: --yolo refuses a ticket that started
without it, since start-ticket posted no Autonomous run comment, which
finish-ticket merges on. It
approves the plan as --approve-plan does, and every line its agents get,
from the start line to the merge line, says "This run is autonomous", so
the skills decide what they would ask, record each decision as an
assumption, and stop at the hard stops workflow.md lists instead of asking
(tkt help lifecycle). A head only the review bot cleared gets review-pr
first, since finish-ticket merges on its verdict alone; then verify-pr
runs, and once its report passes every step the loop sends finish-ticket
the autonomous merge line with tkt merge --autonomous, one merge at a time
in the repository. It waits for finish-ticket after the merge: Status: DONE
ends it with merged, and tkt watch removes the ticket; a failure of the
checks on the base ends it with post_merge_failed and a notification, and
nothing else happens. Steps verify-pr could not run pause it (needs_you).
The ticket stays a yolo one when its loop starts again, and every line tkt
sends it says so, until tkt auto --stop hands it back to you, dropping
any merge order it left. A merge line you send yourself never says the run
is autonomous, so finish-ticket takes your word. tkt ls shows
auto.yolo, and yolo in the AUTO column while the loop drives it.

Where a person decides, the loop pauses instead of ending: when the agent
asks a question or ends with Status: BLOCKED (needs_you), when the plan waits
and --approve-plan is off (plan_awaits_approval), when no agent runs
(agent_missing), when the bot has not reviewed a head after [review] bot_wait
(bot_silent), after [auto] max_rounds fix runs since the plan's approval
(round_limit), when a step would repeat on the same head with nothing
changed (no_progress), when tkt sync cannot merge the base for now, such as
with uncommitted changes in the worktree (sync_failed: it tries again at each
look, and tkt ls says why in auto.note), and while the ticket is on hold
(hold, with no notification). It records the pause, which tkt ls shows as
auto.paused, notifies once with --notify, and goes on by itself when the
ticket moves, such as after you answer the agent in its tab or approve the
plan.

A loop ends only when the ticket is ready for you, merged or closed (with
--yolo, also when the checks on the base fail after the merge), or with
tkt auto --stop, which it notices at its next look. Ctrl-C ends it with exit 5
and leaves the ticket marked for auto, so tkt ls shows auto.wanted. While a
loop drives the ticket, its tab reads ACM-12 (claude, auto).

When tkt update replaces tkt, a loop restarts on the new tkt at its next
look, once its agent stops working: the same process runs the same command
again. It keeps the pause it notified you about, so it does not notify it
twice.

At most [auto] max_parallel tkt auto agents work at once in a repository. A
loop holds a slot while its agent works and gives it up while it waits for CI,
the bot or you. A ticket waiting for a slot shows as queued in tkt ls, even
before it has a worktree.

While a status page that the running tkt watch reads reports an incident
(tkt help watch), the loop sets no agent to work: it starts, approves and
runs nothing, and spends no round, until the incident ends. A sync needs no
agent and goes on. tkt ls shows incident in auto.waiting, and --once says it
waits for the incident. tkt run starts an agent anyway.

--once takes at most one step and exits 0, saying what it did, what it waits
for, or why it would stop or pause. With --dry-run it prints the step instead.
--notify shows a herdr notification when the loop pauses for you or ends.
commands.example:
tkt auto ACM-12 --approve-plan --notify
  tkt auto ACM-12 --yolo --notify
  tkt approve ACM-12 && tkt auto ACM-12
  tkt auto ACM-12 --once
  tkt auto ACM-12 --once --dry-run
  tkt auto ACM-12 --stop

commands.short: Keep the repository's tickets moving: sync moved bases, fix failing checks, remove finished tickets
commands.long:
tkt watch keeps a repository's tickets moving, every ticket and not only the
ones you hand to tkt auto. Every [watch] interval (60s) it fetches, reads
every ticket with a fixed number of gh calls, and takes at most one step per
ticket, from the same rules as tkt ls:

  - finish-ticket ended with Status: DONE after the merge: it runs tkt done,
    unless [watch] done_after_merge = false;
  - the base moved at a moment a sync is due (a conflict, the bot's
    STALE_BASE, BLOCKED_FOR_SYNC behind the base): it merges a clean base
    itself, as tkt sync does, with no agent, and runs resolve on a conflict;
  - the checks fail at the head: it runs ci in a fresh session, once per
    head;
  - a merge order from tkt merge holds at the head, its checks passed and
    review-pr's READY_FOR_HUMAN is at the head: it sends finish-ticket the
    merge line in a fresh session, for one ticket at a time. A base that
    moved gets a sync first, and the order holds across that clean merge.
    A head review-pr has not cleared, such as one a sync made or one only
    the review bot cleared, gets review-pr in a fresh session. A new head
    of any other kind, a failed human verification step, or another
    session taking the ticket over after the line went out drops the
    order, with a notification.

Everything else waits for you or for tkt auto: plans, the other reviews,
findings, human verification and the word to merge. It leaves alone a ticket on hold (tkt
hold), one a tkt auto loop drives, one another tkt command works on, one
whose agent works or asks a question, and one whose worktree directory is
gone. It replaces an agent with a fresh session only after the agent sat
idle for five minutes, since a person may still use that session, and it
waits while the forge still shows an older head than the branch has. A step
it would repeat on the same head, or a fix run past [auto] max_rounds, waits
for you instead: tkt ls shows the ticket as needs_you, with watch.paused
saying why, and herdr notifies once.

Its agent runs take the [auto] max_parallel slots tkt auto uses. It records
each step in the history, and shows a herdr notification for each agent run,
failure and removal; a clean sync stays quiet. A sync that fails, such as
while the network is down, is tried again at the next pass, with one
notification for each head and reason.

It also starts the repository's chores, the agent runs its
.tkt/tkt.local.toml schedules, when their slot comes (tkt help chores): once per slot, however
many slots passed while no watch ran, and never while the chore's last run
is still open. A chore's run is a row like a ticket's: watch syncs its base
when a sync is due, fixes its checks, and removes the run once you merged
its pull request, or once its agent ended with nothing to change.

The [status.NAME] tables in config.toml and the .tkt files name status pages, such as GitHub's
(tkt help config). tkt watch reads them every five minutes. While one
reports a problem with a component that counts, it starts no agent: no ci,
resolve or review run, no merge line and no chore run, since each would only
spend a round on a service that is down. Syncs and removals, which need no
agent, go on, and tkt auto loops wait the same way (tkt help auto). It notifies when an incident starts and when it ends, and tkt
ls and the tkt agent's board show it while it lasts. A page it cannot read
keeps what it said last for fifteen minutes after its last answer, then
holds nothing back.

One tkt watch runs per repository. Every tkt command in a herdr pane starts
it when none runs, in a session of its own, so it outlives the command and the
pane; it writes its lines to watch.log in the repository's git directory,
under tkt/. It waits a minute between two starts, so a watch that exits at
once is not started again by every command. [watch] autostart = false, or
TKT_WATCH=off, turns that off. tkt ls --json says whether it runs, in
watch.running, and watch.error says why its last pass failed. tkt watch
--stop stops it, after the step it is taking; a second SIGTERM stops it at
once. When tkt update replaces tkt, the watch stops by itself, and the next
tkt command starts one that runs the new tkt.

Outside a herdr pane it finds the workspace whose panes work in the
repository. When none has a pane there, it opens one before its first step,
since every step works in herdr. While herdr is down it waits.

--install keeps it running while no terminal is open: it writes systemd user
units, or launchd agents on macOS, for herdr's server and for this
repository's tkt watch, with this shell's PATH, since the agents in herdr's
panes inherit herdr's. It asks before loginctl enable-linger, which keeps
the units running past your last session and starts them at boot; --yes
answers yes, and without a terminal the answer is no. Without linger,
systemd stops the units when your last session ends, so herdr's unit stays
off, since it would take every agent with it, and tkt watch runs from login
to logout. With linger, herdr's unit goes on, and starts unless herdr
already runs. tkt commands then start the unit rather than a watch of their
own, and --stop stops the unit, which signals tkt watch alone, so it
finishes the step it took. --uninstall removes this repository's unit;
herdr's stays. tkt doctor checks that they run and that their PATH finds the
tools and harnesses.

--once takes one pass and exits; with --dry-run it says what each ticket would
get, and changes nothing. --install and --uninstall take --dry-run too.
commands.example:
tkt watch
  tkt watch --once --dry-run
  tkt watch --stop
  tkt watch --install
  tkt watch --uninstall

flags.name: dry-run
flags.usage: with --once, say what each ticket would get instead of doing it; with --install or --uninstall, what would change

flags.name: install

commands.short: Put a ticket on hold, so tkt watch and tkt auto leave it alone
commands.long:
tkt hold puts a ticket on hold: tkt watch and tkt auto leave it alone until
tkt hold ID --off. Use it for a ticket you parked, or one you want to drive by
hand. The commands you run yourself, such as tkt run and tkt sync, still work
on it, and tkt ls still shows its next step.

A tkt auto loop that drives the ticket pauses while it is on hold, without a
notification, and goes on when the hold lifts. tkt ls shows hold in the AUTO
column and hold: true in --json.

The mark lives in the ticket's state, so it goes away with the worktree. tkt
history lists each time a ticket was put on hold and taken off it.
commands.example:
tkt hold ACM-9
  tkt hold ACM-9 --off

commands.short: Replace the ticket's idle agent with a fresh session and send a stage line
commands.long:
tkt run closes the ticket's idle agent and starts a fresh session in the same
pane, on the ticket's preset, then sends the stage's line. The new agent
remembers nothing of the old conversation and does not need to: every stage
reads what it needs from the branch, the pull request and the tracker. Use it
to begin the next stage with a clean context.

Stages:
  review   review-pr reviews the pull request at its head and posts a verdict.
           Run it when the agent ends with Status: READY_FOR_REVIEW.
  address  address-pr-review merges the base into the branch when it moved,
           then fixes the valid findings, answers the rest and pushes. Run it
           when the review asks for changes, you left comments, or the merge
           stopped with Status: HUMAN_QA_FAILED.
  resolve  merges the base when the merge conflicts, resolves each conflict
           from what both sides meant, changes nothing else and pushes once.
           tkt sync starts it on a conflict; for a moved base, run tkt sync
           instead, which merges a clean one with no agent.
  sync     the same line as address, under its old name. tkt run warns, and
           the next release drops it: use tkt sync or address.
  ci       finds why the checks fail at the head, fixes it and pushes once.
  verify   verify-pr runs the pull request's human verification steps at its
           head, in a browser or with each step's commands, and posts what
           it saw for each one as a review. It changes no code. [verify] as
           runs it on another preset (tkt help config).
  start    runs start-ticket again and returns a new plan.

config.toml and the repository's .tkt files can change these lines or add
stages (tkt help config).

A chore's run takes ci, resolve and your own --prompt. It has no ticket, so
tkt run refuses it a stage whose line runs a lifecycle skill, such as
review, address, verify or start, which needs one.

tkt run refuses while the agent works or waits for your answer (tkt wait
blocks until it is done). It also refuses while the ticket is still in
planning, because that agent may hold a plan waiting for your approval;
approve it with tkt approve instead. --force replaces it anyway, and also replaces
an agent in a state tkt does not recognize.
commands.example:
tkt run ACM-12 review
  tkt run ACM-12 review --as big
  tkt run ACM-12 address
  tkt run ACM-12 --prompt "Check the flaky login test again."

commands.short: Merge the base into the ticket's branch: itself when clean, through a fresh session on a conflict
commands.long:
tkt sync brings the ticket's branch up to date with its base, without an
agent whenever it can. It fetches, then merges the base in memory with git
merge-tree, which touches neither the worktree nor the branch:

  - When the merge is clean, tkt makes the merge commit itself and pushes it,
    in seconds. CI and the review bot then run on the new head.
  - When it conflicts, a fresh session runs the resolve stage: it merges the
    base, resolves each conflict from what both sides meant, changes nothing
    else, and pushes once. Review findings stay for address. --no-agent
    stops at the conflict instead, with exit 4.
  - When the branch already contains the base, it does nothing.

It never rebases and never force-pushes. A merge commit tkt made counts as
clean for the review brief: its tree equals what git merge-tree gives for
its two parents, which review-pr checks for itself.

tkt sync refuses while an agent works in the worktree, while the worktree has
uncommitted changes to tracked files (an untracked file does not count),
before the branch is on the remote, and when the branch has commits the
remote lacks, since it pushes only its own merge. When someone pushed to the
branch since the worktree last moved, it fast-forwards first. It pushes the
merge commit it checked, and when the push fails, or you press Ctrl-C, it
takes its merge back off the branch, unless a commit came on top of it
meanwhile: then it leaves the branch alone and says how to drop the merge.

Sync at the moments a ticket needs it: the pull request conflicts, a review
cannot happen because the base moved (the bot's STALE_BASE, or review-pr's
BLOCKED_FOR_SYNC), or a merge is due and finish-ticket stopped with
BLOCKED_FOR_SYNC. tkt ls suggests it then, and tkt auto runs it. Syncing on
every move of the base costs a CI run and a review per ticket for nothing.
commands.example:
tkt sync ACM-12
  tkt sync ACM-12 --dry-run
  tkt sync ACM-12 --no-agent --json

commands.short: Have finish-ticket merge a verified ticket, now or once its checks pass
commands.long:
tkt merge hands a ticket whose human verification passed to finish-ticket.
It sends a fresh session in the ticket's tab the line

  Use the finish-ticket skill to merge the PR. Human verification steps 1
  to 3 passed on head HEAD.

finish-ticket then checks CI, the review and the feedback at the exact
head, merges, moves the ticket to done in the tracker, waits for
post-merge CI, and ends with Status: DONE. tkt watch removes the ticket
after that.

--passed names the steps that passed: numbers and ranges such as 1-3 or
1,2,4, or all. finish-ticket merges only when every step passed, so tkt
merge refuses a list that leaves one out; to waive a step, tell the agent
in the ticket's tab yourself. --head names the head the steps ran on. The
steps hold across clean merges of the base, the ones tkt sync makes, so tkt
merge refuses only a head that changed beyond them. Before any session
starts, it also refuses a base whose merge conflicts (the steps never carry
over a resolution: sync, then verify the new head), a head no review
cleared that no sync made, and failing checks at a head it would merge as
it is.
finish-ticket checks the rest itself.

When finish-ticket could not merge yet, tkt merge leaves a merge order
instead, on the --as preset if you named one, and tkt watch carries it out.
A branch behind its base gets a clean sync first. finish-ticket merges on
review-pr's READY_FOR_HUMAN at the head, so a head a sync made, or one only
the review bot cleared, waits for review-pr, which tkt watch runs. The order
also waits for running checks, and for another ticket's merge, since one
goes at a time: a turn lock covers the moment from tkt merge's check to its
line. The line then names the head the steps passed on
and the one to merge, and finish-ticket checks the merges between them
itself. tkt ls shows the order in the merge field, and the tkt agent's
board as merges when green.

The order stands until the pull request merges. When finish-ticket stops
with BLOCKED_FOR_SYNC because another merge moved the base, tkt watch syncs
again and sends the line on the new head; on one head it sends the line
once. A new head of any other kind, such as a fix or the resolution of a
conflict, drops the order, with a notification, since the steps ran on code
it changed.

--evidence says you confirmed the steps from verify-pr's evidence rather than
by running them. The line then says so, and finish-ticket checks that
verify-pr's report for that head marks each step PASSED. --head defaults to
the head the report ran on, and tkt merge refuses with not_verified when the
report is missing there or marks a step otherwise.

--autonomous merges a yolo ticket, as tkt auto --yolo does: you authorized
the merge when you started the ticket, and verify-pr's report, which must
pass every step on the head it ran on, stands in for the steps. The line
says the run is autonomous, and finish-ticket counts each step as waived,
once it finds start-ticket's Autonomous run comment on the ticket. It
refuses with autonomous_off a ticket tkt auto --yolo did not start, and a
repository whose workflow.md does not turn on autonomous runs.

--cancel drops the order. tkt merge holds the ticket's lock until the line
is sent, so --cancel either drops the order before or finds the line sent:
it then says when, and stopping finish-ticket is up to you, in the
ticket's tab.
commands.example:
tkt merge ACM-12 --passed 1-3
  tkt merge ACM-12 --passed all --head a1b2c3d
  tkt merge ACM-12 --passed all --evidence
  tkt merge ACM-12 --cancel

commands.short: Relaunch the ticket's newest session when no agent runs for it
commands.long:
tkt resume brings back the ticket's last conversation when no agent runs for
it: you closed the tab, the agent exited or crashed, herdr restarted, or the
machine rebooted. It relaunches the newest session (the one tkt recorded,
otherwise the newest Claude Code or OpenCode session in the worktree) in
bypass mode, in the ticket's tab or a new one, and sends nothing, so the agent
waits where it stopped.

Use it instead of tkt run when the conversation matters, such as a plan
waiting for approval. When an agent already runs, tkt resume says where and
changes nothing; --focus switches to its tab.
commands.example:
tkt resume ACM-12
  tkt resume ACM-12 --focus
  tkt resume ACM-12 --session 22222222-2222-2222-2222-222222222222

commands.short: Close a merged ticket's tabs and remove its worktree
commands.long:
tkt done closes the ticket's tabs and removes its worktree, and the private
temporary directory its tabs had as TMPDIR, once its pull request is merged.
worktrunk deletes the branch when it is merged into the base; after a squash
merge the branch stays.

It keeps the worktree, and says why, when:
  - the pull request is still open, or no merged pull request has the branch;
  - the worktree has uncommitted changes;
  - the branch tip is neither the merged head nor in the base;
  - an agent in the worktree works or waits for an answer;
  - tkt runs inside the worktree or in the ticket's own tab;
  - a pane outside the ticket's tabs, or the OpenCode service, works in it.

It removes a chore's run the same way, once you merged its pull request or
closed it, and also one that opened none and holds nothing the base lacks,
as when its agent found nothing to change (tkt help chores).

--all checks every ticket worktree and asks before removing them; pass --yes
when stdin is not a terminal. It reads pull requests through gh, so it
supports GitHub forges only.

It records the merge in the history, so tkt stats can say how long the ticket
took from tkt start to the merge.

finish-ticket ends its report with an Unblocked: line, right before Status:
DONE: the tickets whose blockers are all done now that this one merged.
tkt done reads it from the ticket's session before it closes the tabs, and
names them. tkt ls lists each one, and the tkt agent's board offers to
start it, until tkt start starts it or a week passes.
commands.example:
tkt done ACM-12
  tkt done ACM-12 --dry-run
  tkt done --all --yes

commands.short: List the repository's chores, with their next run
commands.long:
A chore is an agent run you schedule, such as a dependency upgrade. Each run
is a branch and a pull request with no ticket. tkt ships no chores: you
define them in the repository's .tkt/tkt.local.toml, your own file in its
main checkout, so each person's chores run once (tkt help config):

  [chores.deps]
  schedule = "0 9 * * 1,4"     # cron's five fields, in local time
  branch = "deps-{date}"       # {name}, {date} and {time}; the default is {name}-{date}
  as = "fast"                  # the preset; leave out for the default
  prompt = "Upgrade the dependencies. Read each migration guide, and note the breaking changes in the pull request."

That repository's tkt watch starts a run when its slot comes. A run gets a
branch from the base on the remote, its own worktree and tab, and an agent
with the chore's prompt and one rule: commit on the run's branch, push it,
open one pull request to the base, and end with Status: READY_FOR_REVIEW
once it is open, or with Status: DONE, committing nothing, when there is
nothing to change. The run's id is its branch, such as deps-2026-10-26: tkt
ls lists it beside the tickets, and tkt run, sync, show, send, hold, resume,
wait, history and done take it.

From there tkt watch treats the pull request as it does a ticket's: it
merges a moved base when a sync is due, and runs ci once per head when the
checks fail. No skill reviews, fixes or merges a pull request without a
ticket, so tkt ls says when the review bot found something, and when the
pull request is ready for you to merge. Merge it yourself, or close it to
drop the run; tkt watch then removes the run, and removes at once a run that
ended with nothing to change. tkt run refuses a run the stages that need a
ticket, such as review and address, and tkt approve, tkt auto and tkt merge
take tickets only.

A run whose start stopped before its agent got the prompt, as at a startup
dialog or on a pre-start hook that failed, waits for you and holds the
chore's next slots: tkt chore run NAME goes on with it in its worktree, and
tkt done drops it. A run never takes the branch of an older one, or of any
pull request, since tkt finds a run's pull request by its branch.

A prompt that runs a slash command, such as /upgrade-dependencies, goes
alone and on one line, since the command would read the rule as its
arguments: the command says how the run ends, and a run that ends with
neither a pull request nor Status: DONE waits for you.

A slot that passes while the chore's last run is still open is skipped, so
one run waits for you at a time. A slot missed while no tkt watch ran runs
once when one runs again, however many passed. The first tkt watch to see a
chore starts its first run at its next slot. While a status page reports an
incident, a due run waits, as every agent run does (tkt help watch).

tkt chores lists the repository's chores: the next slot, the last one tkt
watch took or skipped, and the run still open. tkt chore run NAME starts a
run now, and refuses while the chore's last run is open, unless that run's
start stopped before its agent got the prompt: then it goes on with it.

A chore that needs no agent, such as npx skills update, belongs in a plain
systemd timer or cron job, without tkt.
commands.example:
tkt chores
  tkt chores --json

commands.short: List ticket worktrees with their state and the next step
commands.long:
tkt ls lists every ticket worktree, or the tickets given, with its phase and
how long it has been there (TIME), its agent, pull request, checks, review
verdict, what tkt auto does with it, and the next step. On a terminal the
phase is colored by who acts next: yellow for you, green when it is ready for
you to verify, cyan while an agent works.

The agent column says working, idle, blocked (it asks a question), or waiting
when it is idle but waits on a background task of its own, such as a CI
watcher, and goes on by itself. tkt reads the agent's last Status: line and
its background tasks from the session's own record, the Claude Code
transcript or the OpenCode API; when tkt cannot read that, from the agent's
recent output.

The next step is the first of these rules that matches:
  1. The pull request is merged: tkt done ID.
  2. The agent works, or waits on its background task: wait; or it waits for
     an answer: answer it.
  3. No pull request yet: tkt resume ID when no agent runs; otherwise read the
     plan and approve it (tkt show ID, tkt approve ID), read the agent's
     reason, or check the agent in its tab.
  4. The agent ended with Status: BLOCKED or SETUP_REQUIRED, or a review
     draft waits for your approval: do it in the tab.
  5. The checks are pending: wait for CI.
  6. The review says the base moved, the pull request conflicts, or the agent
     said BLOCKED_FOR_SYNC with the branch behind the base: tkt sync ID, which
     merges a clean base itself and hands a conflict to a fresh session.
  7. The merge stopped with HUMAN_QA_FAILED, verify-pr's report for the head
     failed a step, or the review at the head has findings: tkt run ID
     address.
  8. The checks fail: tkt run ID ci.
  9. The review at the head is clear, from the bot or from review-pr. When
     verify-pr's report for the head passed every step: confirm them from
     its evidence, then tkt merge ID --passed all --evidence. When it could
     not run some: run those yourself. Otherwise tkt run ID verify, which
     workflow.md's Agent verification row makes the step, or the steps
     yourself. A report counts for the head it ran on, and across clean
     merges of the base after it.
 10. No review at the head yet: without a bot ([review] bot_wait = "0s"),
     tkt run ID review. With one, wait bot_wait for it, counted from when tkt
     first saw the head waiting; after that, check the bot's CI job.

A verdict on an older head does not count, so after every push the next step
waits for a new review.

A chore's run is a row too, named by its branch (tkt help chores). No skill
reviews, fixes or merges a pull request without a ticket, so some rules
differ for it: an agent that ended with Status: DONE and no pull request
found nothing to change, and a pull request you closed drops the run (tkt
done ID, for both); a start that stopped before the agent got its prompt
goes on with tkt chore run NAME; findings in the review at the head are
yours to read; and a green pull request that the bot cleared, or did not
review within bot_wait, is yours to merge.

With --json each row's next step is an object whose argv, when set, is the
command to run, and whose reason names the rule: merged, closed,
agent_working, agent_waiting, agent_blocked, no_agent, plan_awaits_approval,
status_blocked, check_agent, review_awaits_approval, ci_pending, base_moved,
qa_failed, verify_failed, findings, checks_fail, needs_verify, verified,
verify_incomplete, autonomous_merge, bot_clear, review_clear, awaiting_bot,
bot_silent, needs_review, no_changes, chore_findings, chore_ready, or, for a
ticket whose tkt auto loop waits before the ticket has a worktree,
awaiting_slot while it waits for a slot and incident while a status page's
incident lasts. Each row also carries chore, the chore's name for a
chore's run; title, the open pull request's title without the ticket id;
diff, what the branch changes against its base; and verification,
verify-pr's newest report with each step's result, whose at_head and
carried say whether it counts for the head. incidents lists what
the status pages report while a tkt watch reads them.

The phase names where a ticket stands: queued, starting, planning,
awaiting_approval, building, ci, waiting_review, reviewing, needs_fix, fixing,
verifying, working, needs_you, ready_for_human, merged, closed, no_agent, or
finished for a chore's run that found nothing to change.
tkt ls records a phase when it sees it change, in the worktree and in the
history tkt stats reads, so the time in a phase is as exact as how often
something runs tkt ls or tkt auto. An agent that sits idle with no status line
longer than [board] stale_after is marked stale.

A yolo ticket (tkt auto --yolo) differs at rule 9: a head only the bot
cleared gets tkt run ID review first, then tkt run ID verify, and once
verify-pr passed every step, tkt merge ID --autonomous (autonomous_merge).

The AUTO column says on while a tkt auto loop drives the ticket, yolo while a
tkt auto --yolo loop does, paused while
it waits for you (auto.paused and auto.why in --json say why), queued while it
waits for a slot, stalled when the ticket is marked for auto but no loop runs,
and hold while the ticket is on hold (tkt hold).

tkt ls reads pull requests through gh, so outside GitHub forges those columns
show ? and nothing is recorded.

tkt ls
  tkt ls ACM-12 --json
  tkt ls --json | jq -r '.result.rows[] | select(.next.kind == "command") | .next.text'

commands.short: Print the agent's last message, its live screen, or the verification steps
commands.long:
tkt show prints the agent's last message: after start-ticket, the plan; after
tkt run ID verify, its report. It reads the message from the session's own
record, the Claude Code transcript or the OpenCode API, so nothing scrolls
away. When tkt cannot read that record, it prints the agent's recent output.

--screen prints the agent's live screen instead, such as a question it asks
in a dialog. --ansi keeps the screen's colors as ANSI escapes, as the tkt
agent's web page draws them.

--diff prints what the branch changes since it left its base, as git diff
prints it: the committed change its pull request shows, against the base as
the last fetch left it. With --json, files lists each file with its status,
the lines it adds and removes, and its hunks.

--steps prints the human verification procedure from the review that says
READY_FOR_HUMAN at the pull request's head, and with --json its numbered
steps. When the review bot cleared the head instead, it reads the Human
verification section of the pull request's body, which work-ticket writes;
source says which. It reads pull requests through gh, so it supports GitHub
forges only, and it exits 4 with no_verification_steps when neither has
steps. When verify-pr reported on the pull request, it prints the report's
result for each step after the procedure, and says when the report is about
an older head; with --json, verification holds it.

tkt show ACM-12
  tkt show ACM-12 --screen
  tkt show ACM-12 --steps --json
  tkt show ACM-12 --diff

until it has finished or needs you, then prints its state and the last
Status: line it wrote since your last message. --until picks other states.

A program that drives tkt waits with it instead of polling tkt ls. With
--timeout, a wait that runs out ends with exit 4 and the code wait_timeout.
--notify shows a herdr notification when the wait ends.
commands.example:
tkt wait ACM-12
  tkt wait ACM-12 --timeout 30m --json
  tkt wait ACM-12 --until blocked

commands.short: Show how long tickets took from start to merge, and how long they waited for you
commands.long:
tkt stats reads the history tkt keeps in ${XDG_STATE_HOME:-~/.local/state}/tkt/history.jsonl
and shows, for this repository's tickets, how long each took from tkt start to
the merge, how much of that it waited for you (a plan to approve, a question,
the human verification), and how many address and ci rounds it needed.
Tickets still in progress show their time so far. The summary gives the
median and the 90th percentile of the merged ones.

tkt records the start and the merge exactly: the start when tkt start first
starts the ticket, the merge from the forge when tkt done removes it. Time in
each phase is as exact as the commands that watch it: tkt ls, tkt auto and the
tkt agent's board record a phase when they see it change.

The history outlives worktrees and only grows. Tickets started before tkt
kept a history have no recorded start and are left out.
commands.example:
tkt stats
  tkt stats --since 720h
  tkt stats ACM-12 --json

flags.name: all-repos
flags.usage: include the tickets of every repository in the history

flags.name: since
flags.usage: only tickets started within DURATION, such as 720h for 30 days

commands.short: Show what happened to tickets: their events, commits and reviews
commands.long:
tkt history shows what happened to each ticket you name, oldest first: every
event in the history tkt keeps in ${XDG_STATE_HOME:-~/.local/state}/tkt/history.jsonl
(the start, each phase, the plan's approval, each stage run, what tkt auto did
and why it stopped, the merge), and the timeline tkt stats counts from them.

On a GitHub forge, it also reads each pull request of the ticket's branch
through gh: its title, size, commits and reviews. A review's verdict and the
head it names come from review-pr's Verdict: line or the review bot's
summary, and the body holds its findings. Reviews with only line comments
and no body are left out. When gh fails, tkt warns, prints the history
alone, and forge says failed.

A ticket keeps its history after tkt done removes its worktree, so this
works for merged tickets too. tkt history is read only. The tkt agent reads it
to answer how a ticket went.
commands.example:
tkt history ACM-12
  tkt history ACM-12 ACM-13 --json

commands.short: Check the tools, versions and configuration tkt needs
commands.long:
tkt doctor checks what the other commands need and reports each check as ok,
warn, fail or skip: git, worktrunk and herdr at their minimum versions, the
herdr pane, gh when the forge is GitHub, the harness of every preset, the
project's lifecycle configuration, config.toml and the repository's .tkt
files, worktrunk's hooks and the log directory. It exits 3 when a check fails.

On a terminal it groups the checks, colors them and ends with a summary.
Otherwise, and with --json, it prints the plain format that programs read.
commands.example:
tkt doctor
  tkt doctor --json

commands.short: Give OpenCode agents their ticket's TMPDIR, and move the /tmp paths they type into it
commands.long:
tkt hook tmp keeps the temporary files of OpenCode agents apart, one ticket
from another. OpenCode runs every agent's tools in its one background
service, so the TMPDIR tkt gives a ticket's tab never reaches them, and two
agents that write /tmp/pr-body.md overwrite each other. Claude Code needs
none of this: it runs its tools in the ticket's tab, under its TMPDIR.

tkt hook tmp --install writes tkt's plugin into OpenCode's global plugins
directory, ~/.config/opencode/plugins/tkt.js, next to the plugins herdr and
others install there. OpenCode loads it when its service starts. In a
ticket's worktree, the plugin asks tkt hook tmp about every tool call and
shell, and

  - gives each shell the ticket's own TMPDIR, the directory tkt start made;
  - moves a new path under /tmp into that directory when a file tool names
    it, or a shell command uses it unquoted, at the start of a word or after
    =: /tmp/notes.md becomes $TMPDIR/notes.md, and later calls find it there;
  - adds a line to the agent's system prompt that says so, and that quotes
    keep a path as written, since an agent that does not expect the move
    fights it.

A path stays when /tmp holds its name already, such as a file you put
there, when the name is one other programs own (a hidden name, a tkt-
directory, Claude Code's and OpenCode's own), and when it is a bare /tmp.
In a shell command, a path stays in quotes, where it is as often a search
pattern or a message as a place; in here-documents and here-strings, which
are data or another program's script; in arithmetic; after a colon, as on
another host; and inside an option, as in -o/tmp/x. A name moves everywhere
in the command or nowhere, so a command never reads from one place what it
wrote to the other. The content and text fields of a tool call stay as
written, and only the shell and the file tools (read, write, edit, glob,
grep, list, patch) are touched: another tool may run its command or name
its path on another machine. Outside a ticket's worktree the plugin changes
nothing, except a TMPDIR that names a ticket's directory: a service started
in a ticket's tab passes that one to its shells, and tkt done removes it.

Without --install, tkt hook tmp answers one request from the plugin: JSON
on stdin with the call's directories, its shell's TMPDIR, and its tool
input or shell command; --json prints the answer. tkt doctor warns when a
preset runs OpenCode and the plugin is missing or comes from another tkt.
commands.example:
tkt hook tmp --install
  echo '{"directories": ["'$PWD'"], "command": "cat > /tmp/pr-body.md"}' | tkt hook tmp

flags.usage: with --install, print the change instead of making it

commands.short: Describe every command, flag, result and error code as JSON
commands.long:
tkt schema prints a JSON description of tkt for programs that drive it: every
command with its arguments, flags and result fields, the exit statuses and
error codes, and the environment variables tkt reads. It is built from the same
definitions as the help, so the two always agree.

Without --json it prints the description itself; with --json it is the result
of the usual envelope.
commands.example:
tkt schema
  tkt schema --json | jq '.result.errors[] | select(.exit == 4) | .code'

commands.short: Replace tkt with the latest release, or with VERSION
commands.long:
tkt update replaces the running tkt with the latest full release from
git.rogs.me, or with the release VERSION names. It downloads the binary for
this system and the release's SHA256SUMS, checks the checksum, runs the new
binary once with --version, and only then renames it over the old one. If a
step fails, the old binary stays. The checksum catches a broken download, not
a compromised host.

Without VERSION, tkt update does nothing when tkt is already at the latest
release or newer. The latest release skips prereleases; name one, such as
v0.3.0-rc.1, to install it. A named VERSION also installs an older release.

A development build, whose tkt --version prints dev, has no version to
compare, so tkt update replaces it only with --force. A go build inside a git
checkout prints a version such as v0.2.1-0.20261019212235-569e7a5572c4, which
counts as newer than v0.2.0. --check reports what tkt update would do and
changes nothing. When tkt runs through a symlink, tkt update
replaces the file the link points to.

Running loops move to the new tkt by themselves: every tkt auto loop
restarts on it at its next look, and tkt watch stops so that its service, or
the next tkt command, starts the new one. The tkt agent's chat runs the old
tkt until you reopen it.
commands.example:
tkt update
  tkt update --check
  tkt update v0.3.0-rc.1

flags.usage: report whether a release would replace tkt, and change nothing

flags.name: force
flags.usage: replace a development build, or reinstall the same version

commands.short: Generate the autocompletion script for bash
commands.long:
Generate the autocompletion script for the bash shell.

This script depends on the 'bash-completion' package.
If it is not installed already, you can install it via your OS's package manager.

To load completions in your current shell session:

	source <(tkt completion bash)

To load completions for every new session, execute once:

#### Linux:

	tkt completion bash > /etc/bash_completion.d/tkt

#### macOS:

	tkt completion bash > $(brew --prefix)/etc/bash_completion.d/tkt

You will need to start a new shell for this setup to take effect.

flags.name: no-descriptions
flags.usage: disable completion descriptions

commands.short: Generate the autocompletion script for zsh
commands.long:
Generate the autocompletion script for the zsh shell.

If shell completion is not already enabled in your environment you will need
to enable it.  You can execute the following once:

	echo "autoload -U compinit; compinit" >> ~/.zshrc

To load completions in your current shell session:

	source <(tkt completion zsh)

To load completions for every new session, execute once:

#### Linux:

	tkt completion zsh > "${fpath[1]}/_tkt"

#### macOS:

	tkt completion zsh > $(brew --prefix)/share/zsh/site-functions/_tkt

You will need to start a new shell for this setup to take effect.

environment.name: TKT_FORMAT
environment.description: json makes every command print the JSON envelope; text, or unset, prints text

environment.name: XDG_CONFIG_HOME
environment.description: tkt reads $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/tkt/config.toml (default ~/.config/tkt/config.toml), then the repository's .tkt/tkt.toml and .tkt/tkt.local.toml

environment.name: XDG_STATE_HOME
environment.description: tkt logs every command it runs to $XDG_STATE_HOME/tkt/tkt.log, and keeps the history tkt stats reads in history.jsonl next to it, and the light or dark choice of the tkt agent's web page in web.json (default ~/.local/state/tkt)

environment.name: XDG_DATA_HOME
environment.description: tkt unpacks its bundled pi and its extension under $XDG_DATA_HOME/tkt (default ~/.local/share/tkt)

environment.name: HERDR_ENV
environment.description: herdr sets it to 1 inside its panes; agent, start, approve, send, auto, run, resume, done, show and wait need it, and tkt alone opens the agent only there

environment.name: HERDR_WORKSPACE_ID
environment.description: the herdr workspace where tkt opens tabs

environment.name: HERDR_TAB_ID
environment.description: the tab tkt runs in; tkt done refuses to close it

environment.name: HERDR_PANE_ID
environment.description: the pane tkt runs in; tkt never starts an agent in it

environment.name: TKT_RELEASES

environment.name: TKT_RELEASES_API
environment.description: the Gitea API that tkt update asks for the latest release (default https://git.rogs.me/api/v1/repos/rogs/tkt)

environment.name: TKT_PI
